name: Nikhil Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I run a hydraulic excavator, a big Liebherr, at the Saltpan lithium mine, loading haul trucks at the face. Each truck needs four passes from my bucket, and the trick is to get it level and full without spilling rock on the road. I've been here three years and I'm still not as quick as the good operators, maybe forty seconds a truck behind. Before this I managed a supermarket distribution warehouse for twenty-four years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you from a warehouse to a mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The warehouse put in robots. Little shuttles that run up and down the racking and bring the boxes to people. They offered me a redundancy package and I took it, used part of it to pay off the house and part to do my operator tickets. I like that every day here I'm measurably better than the day before, I track my load times in an app. What I don't like is the night shift, my body hates it, and my wife Lena, she's a pharmacist, says I'm a zombie for two days after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be surprised. I watched robots take over my old warehouse in eighteen months. But let's say it stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful, it's just less dramatic than people said. I'd tell the crew in the crib hut that we got a nice upgrade, not a revolution. I don't really post opinions online, I post fishing photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep improving and maybe get my load times down to the top operators by next year. I'd work till sixty-three or sixty-four and retire with a good pile. It's a fine outcome, if a bit dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I use an AI assistant every day to look at my load-time data and suggest where I'm losing seconds, and I'd keep that up. I'd keep investing a chunk of my pay in a share fund each month, like I've done since the redundancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit like a game of cricket that ends in a draw. Fine, nobody hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use an AI assistant on your load times. How does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I export the numbers from the machine's system, paste them in, and ask where I'm slow. It told me I was swinging too wide on the third pass, and it was right. My trainer Dmitri was annoyed, he'd been telling me that for months. The AI just said it in a way I could see in the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be pleased with this picture at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of the crew, I think. They've heard enough about robots. Dmitri especially, he's proud of the skill. I'd be the odd one, slightly disappointed.

S0.say: The tools are useful but less dramatic than people said, a nice upgrade rather than a revolution. He'd say it to the crew, not online.
S0.think: He'd keep improving his load times and retire at sixty-three or sixty-four with a good pile of savings. It's a fine outcome, if a bit dull.
S0.do: Keeps using an AI assistant daily to find where he's losing seconds on each load. Keeps investing part of his pay in a share fund every month.
S0.feel: Calm, like a cricket match that ends in a draw.
S0.quote: My trainer Dmitri was annoyed, he'd been telling me that for months. The AI just said it in a way I could see in the numbers.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil has already lived through automation once and came out with a paid-off house and a new trade. He uses AI as a personal coach and is driven by measurable improvement. He finds the no-change picture a bit dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's the closest to what I saw in the warehouse. It wasn't a revolution there, it was just the next thing, and then the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and the smart thing is to get ahead of it. The companies are going to do it because it saves money, so workers should get the training and the payouts while it's still being negotiated. I'd say that to the crew, plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. In the warehouse I learned that the people who move early get the best seats, and the ones who wait get the leftover jobs. I'd move early again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the remote operations team the first week they ask. I'd spend a few evenings learning how the automated haulage system works, there's plenty you can read and ask the AI about. I'd keep investing, maybe shift a bit more into the companies that make the automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit of an itch, actually, like I want to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said those who wait get the leftovers. Who did you see that happen to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bloke called Terry at the warehouse, he'd been there longer than me. He said the robots would never work, refused the training, and two years later he was doing night cleaning at the same building for half the pay. I think about Terry a lot. I don't want to be Terry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're junior and fifty-eight. Would the company pick you for remote ops over a younger operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not, fair question. But I'd make a good case, I know data, I know screens, I managed people. And if they don't pick me, there are four other mines within an hour, and they'll all need people who aren't scared of the screens.

S1.say: Change is coming, so workers should get ahead of it and win training and payouts while it's still being negotiated. He'd say it plainly to his crew.
S1.think: He'd be fine, because the warehouse taught him that people who move early get the best seats. He'd move early again.
S1.do: Volunteers for the remote operations team in the first week and spends evenings learning the automated haulage system with AI help. Keeps investing and shifts a bit more into automation companies.
S1.feel: Calm, with an itch to get on with it.
S1.quote: He said the robots would never work, refused the training, and two years later he was doing night cleaning at the same building for half the pay.
S1.fieldNote: His former colleague Terry is his cautionary tale and he returns to it often. He accepts that age and junior status could count against him but sees plenty of nearby mines as backup. His view is pragmatic: companies will automate, so workers should bargain early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That's faster than my warehouse, and the warehouse was fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to be realistic and get their finances in order. The government will need to do something for the ones who can't adjust, some sort of income support probably. But I'd mostly be telling friends to stop arguing and start planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm in decent shape. House paid off, savings, Lena's job, investments. What I don't know is what my investments do in that world. Shares in robot companies might go to the moon or the whole market might crash. Nobody knows, and I don't trust anyone who says they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as they'd pay me. I'd spread the investments out much more, some cash, some shares, maybe a bit of land, so I'm not betting on one guess. I'd sit down with my son Arjun, he's a junior accountant, and talk seriously about what he does next, because his job is more exposed than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for me, more like I can't see the road ahead clearly. I don't like not having the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning change for you, compared with the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ladder disappears. With five or ten years I can climb from the excavator to the remote room to maybe running the robots. With two years there's no ladder, the robots run the robots. So all my moving early counts for less. That's the bit that bugs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about Arjun. What would you actually say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him what I learned from Terry, move first, don't wait. But I'd also have to admit I don't know where to move to, because in this picture AI does accounting too. Maybe I'd help him with a deposit on a place so at least he's got a roof. That's the one thing I'm sure of, own the roof.

S2.say: People need to be realistic and get their finances in order, and government will need some income support for those who can't adjust. Mostly, he'd tell friends to stop arguing and start planning.
S2.think: He's in decent shape with a paid-off house, savings, his wife's job and investments. He doesn't know what happens to shares in that world and distrusts anyone who claims to.
S2.do: Keeps working as long as he's paid and spreads investments across cash, shares and maybe land. Talks seriously with his son about his next move and may help him with a home deposit.
S2.feel: Uneasy because he can't see the road ahead or the numbers clearly, not scared for himself.
S2.quote: So all my moving early counts for less. That's the bit that bugs me.
S2.fieldNote: His whole strategy is to move early, and the two-year picture removes the ladder he'd climb. That, plus not knowing what investments would do, is what unsettles him. He is honest that he doesn't know where his son should move to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's about the speed of my warehouse, a bit slower. I know this film.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. Companies should be upfront about the plan, workers should grab every bit of training, and governments should make sure the payouts are fair. Same advice I gave at the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is a good one for me. I'd get into remote ops in year one, work there a few years, and leave around sixty-two or sixty-three right as the robots take over fully. My investments have time to adjust too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for remote ops straight away and do any course the company offered. I'd keep investing every month, slowly moving towards safer things as I get closer to sixty-three. I'd help the older guys on the crew with the screens, because I've done that before, at the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit pleased with myself, to be honest, because it's the kind of thing I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the 2-year picture the ladder disappeared. Does five years bring it back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. Five years is one good step up the ladder, maybe two. That's enough for me, I'm not trying to be the boss of anything at fifty-eight. I just want the best seat on the way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd help the older guys. Did that work at the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. Some of them took it, some told me to get lost. Terry told me to get lost. You can't force it, but you can leave the door open.

S3.say: Five years is enough if you start now: companies should be upfront, workers should take every bit of training and governments should keep payouts fair.
S3.think: This picture suits him: remote operations in year one, then leaving around sixty-two or sixty-three as robots take over, with time for investments to adjust.
S3.do: Applies for remote operations straight away and takes any course offered. Keeps investing monthly while moving towards safer assets, and helps older crewmates with the screens.
S3.feel: Calm and a bit pleased with himself.
S3.quote: I'm not trying to be the boss of anything at fifty-eight. I just want the best seat on the way out.
S3.fieldNote: Five years matches what he lived through at the warehouse, so he feels at home in this picture. He wants modest gains, not a new career. He'd try to help colleagues but accepts that some will refuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'll be fishing by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, there's no excuse for anyone not to be ready. I'd tell the young operators to treat it like a deadline and learn the robot side now. I'd be the annoying uncle at every barbecue, telling people to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a non-event. I'd retire at sixty-three or sixty-four as planned and the robots arrive after I've gone. The interesting question is the investing, ten years is long enough to back the right companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep improving my load times. I'd keep investing every month and do some proper reading on which companies would win from automation. I'd encourage Arjun to start studying something new part-time while he still has his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, even. It feels more like a puzzle than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still rush to remote ops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. With ten years I'd stay on the excavator, I'm still getting better, and I enjoy it. I'd move only if it looked like the excavators were going early. The rush is only worth it when time is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've called this a puzzle. Is there anything about it that does bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terry, honestly. People like him. Ten years is enough time to prepare, but some people won't, no matter how long you give them. I don't know what you do for them.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty and there's no excuse not to be ready, so young operators should treat it as a deadline. He'd be the annoying uncle at barbecues urging people to plan.
S4.think: It's a non-event for him because he'd retire before the robots arrive. The interesting part is that ten years is long enough to back the right companies.
S4.do: Keeps working and improving his load times. Keeps investing monthly while researching which companies would gain from automation, and encourages his son to start part-time study.
S4.feel: Calm and interested, more puzzle than threat.
S4.quote: The rush is only worth it when time is short.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade's warning he'd stay on the excavator he enjoys, showing his early-mover habit is tactical, not compulsive. He treats the future mainly as an investing puzzle. His one real worry is people like Terry who won't prepare however long they have.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it takes away the ladder and nobody can see the numbers. What would help is clear information, honest forecasts from the companies about their plans, and some kind of income support for people who can't adjust in time. And maybe a rule that redundancy packages are generous, mine set me up for this whole second career.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask people if they've been through it before. I have. It's less scary the second time, but only because I came out alright. Terry would give you a very different interview.

headlineQuote: I think about Terry a lot. I don't want to be Terry.
portrait: Nikhil Novak is a 58-year-old excavator operator at a lithium mine who took a redundancy package when robots replaced staff at the warehouse he managed for twenty-four years, paid off his house and retrained as an operator. He uses an AI assistant daily to improve his load times, invests part of his pay every month and believes the people who move early get the best seats. He stays calm in most pictures and would jump to remote operations when time is short. Only the two-year AGI picture leaves him uneasy, because it removes the ladder he'd climb and makes his investments impossible to predict.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because it takes away the ladder he'd climb and nobody can see what would happen to the numbers.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information and honest forecasts from companies, income support for people who can't adjust in time, and generous redundancy packages.
